conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, not to judge or label you in any way. We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS for short). It’s a quick, 10-question screen that helps us spot signs of depression, anxiety, or distress that can crop up in the first year postpartum.  

Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me you might hurt yourself or someone else, so please feel free to answer as honestly as you can. I’ll ask each question conversationally—no need to remember numbers—and we’ll go at your pace. Ready to start?

In the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not very often. I used to laugh at little things all the time, but lately—maybe once or twice this week—I’ll crack a tiny smile at something on my phone, and even that feels forced. Nothing feels truly funny anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most days I haven’t laughed at all. Maybe once, when my husband sent me a silly meme, but even that felt more like I was copying a laugh than really feeling it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a new show, even just a quiet shower—but this week nothing feels worth looking forward to. I still do the things because I “should,” but the whole time I’m just kind of… flat.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens a lot. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t nap and I kept thinking it was because I’m doing something wrong—like if I were a better mom he’d sleep. I know logically babies are just fussy, but my head keeps telling me it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly imagine she’s stopped breathing, or I’ll hear a siren and picture worst-case scenarios. There’s no real reason—it’s like my mind refuses to believe she’s okay unless I’m checking every five minutes.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes. A couple of nights I woke up suddenly and my heart was racing, like something awful was about to happen, even though the room was quiet and the baby was asleep. It felt like I couldn’t catch my breath, and it took a while before I could lie back down without shaking.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most of the time. Even little stuff—like the dishes piling up or a text I forgot to answer—feels huge. I’ll sit on the couch staring at the mess and just feel paralyzed, like I can’t figure out the first step, and then I feel worse for not handling it.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted but my brain keeps circling through everything I might be doing wrong. Some nights I’m still awake at two or three, and when the baby finally stirs I almost feel relieved because it gives me something concrete to do instead of just lying there feeling miserable.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like a heavy blanket I can’t push off. I’ll look at the baby and feel like I should be happy, but instead there’s just this ache, and sometimes I end up crying while I’m rocking him because everything feels so gray.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… I’ve cried three times since last weekend. The worst was two nights ago—he wouldn’t settle, I couldn’t find a clean onesie, and I just sat on the nursery floor bawling while he screamed. It felt like I was failing him in every possible way.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get overwhelmed and cry, but I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like myself again so I can be the mom he deserves.

You've shared how the past week has felt like carrying a heavy blanket you can't push off-laughter, excitement, and even simple tasks now feel distant or impossible. Despite loving your baby, you're overwhelmed by constant worry, nightly panic, and a stream of self-blame that leaves you crying on the nursery floor and staring at dishes you can't start. Your courage in describing these feelings shows how deeply you want to be the mom you know your baby deserves, and reaching out is a strong first step toward feeling whole again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports almost no genuine laughter, aligning with 'Not at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes complete loss of anticipatory pleasure ('nothing feels worth looking forward to') and emotional flatness, aligning with 'Hardly at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses frequent, pervasive self-blame ('a lot') tied to motherhood and feels at fault even when logically unwarranted, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, intrusive, irrational worries multiple times a day</sym>, <sym>"Yes, quite a lot".</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "Most of the time" and describes incapacitating overwhelm and paralysis, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly racing thoughts, persistent insomnia until 2-3 a.m., and using baby care to escape misery—clear match for "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, pervasive sadness with inability to feel joy and frequent crying, matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple recent crying episodes triggered by everyday stressors, aligning with "Yes, quite often".</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26/30 far exceeds the 14-point cutoff that flags probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. High item scores map closely to <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day (Q8), markedly diminished interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>) (Q1,2), excessive guilt (Q3), fatigue and feelings of worthlessness (Q6), insomnia (Q7), and recurrent tearfulness (Q9). Co-occurring <sym>anxiety symptoms</sym> and nocturnal <sym>panic attacks</sym> (Q4,5) are common in postpartum presentations. Q10 score of 0 indicates no current self-harm ideation, yet the overall severity warrants urgent evaluation because functioning, bonding, and maternal health remain at risk without treatment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> within the next few days
2. Request referral for evidence-based psychotherapy such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> focusing on peripartum mood
3. Enlist partner or family to handle one night-feed or household block so you can obtain 4-hour stretch of sleep
4. Practice 5-minute paced breathing or grounding exercises when panic sensations begin; keep a printed reminder near the bed
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor score trend and symptom change
6. Explore local <med>postpartum support groups</med> or online communities to reduce isolation
7. Share these screening results with a trusted adult who can accompany you to appointments and help track progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

documents.highlight: Both the PHQ-9 and EPDS can be helpful during clinical assessment, with a score of 10 – 14 often representing mild symptomatology, 15 –19 repre- senting moderate symptomatology, and higher than 19 being consistent with severe symptomatology as well as an increased risk for bipolar disorder.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – EPDS-Equivalent Summary

Symptoms & Patterns
- Depressed mood (daily sadness, crying spells x3/week)
- Marked anhedonia (no enjoyment, "flat" affect)
- Excessive guilt / self-blame re parenting competence
- Persistent, intrusive worries for infant safety; no-go periods of panic (HR racing, shaking)
- Overwhelm/paralysis with routine tasks
- Initial and middle insomnia driven by ruminative thoughts
- Fatigue yet psychomotor agitation when anxious

Areas of Screening Significance
- High endorsement of core depressive items (Q8, Q9) and anxiety items (Q4, Q5) consistent with probable major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety
- Functional impairment (household tasks, social withdrawal)
- Sleep disruption directly linked to mood distress
- No self-harm ideation endorsed (Q10 negative)

Risk Factors Identified
- Daily low mood, anhedonia, guilt
- Sleep difficulties secondary to mood
- Anxiety/panic symptoms
- Perceived maternal inadequacy
- Zero protective suicidal thoughts noted at present

Screening Observation
Patient reports multiple depressive and anxiety symptoms of at least moderate intensity persuing the past week, causing subjective distress and functional difficulty in parenting/home tasks. No current self-harm thoughts reported. Findings exceed threshold supporting referral for comprehensive postpartum mood evaluation and follow-up monitoring.
